news.title: Musk and other tech leaders back petition urging Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
news.summary: A petition asking Nvidia's board to bring Huang back while an independent investigation runs passed 115,000 signatures by Saturday. Elon Musk, Replit's Amjad Masad and Epic's Tim Sweeney are among the supporters, who argue he was pushed out without fair process.

news.title: Asian governments respond unevenly to Huang's exit from Nvidia
news.summary: South Korea says Nvidia reaffirmed its GPU supply plans, Japan says it is watching closely, and Taiwan says the Taipei headquarters project is on track. China rejected the spying allegations tied to a businesswoman linked to Huang.

news.title: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team
news.summary: Fortune reports OpenAI has folded its robotics researchers into its core research and applied groups, betting its general-purpose models can run robots directly. OpenAI says it remains committed to robotics and is still building its own humanoid.

news.title: Founders and VCs brace for a smaller Nvidia checkbook after Huang's departure
news.summary: Investors expect Nvidia to be more selective with startup bets under interim CEO Colette Kress, which could mean smaller rounds and lower valuations across AI. Some hope cloud giants and rival chipmakers will fill the gap.

news.title: Anthropic's IPO reportedly draws about six times more orders than shares
news.summary: Citing Bloomberg, Reuters reports the offering is roughly six times oversubscribed and could be the largest first-time share sale on record. Anthropic is expected to price on Nov. 18 and start trading on Nasdaq as ANT on Nov. 19, with existing backers likely prioritized.

news.title: Chinese AI firms reportedly rush to lock in overseas compute
news.summary: Chinese AI companies are said to be signing foreign compute deals out of fear that US lawmakers will curb remote access to advanced chips after the Nvidia spy case. Such rules could move after the midterm elections.

news.title: LangChain raises $300M at a $3B valuation
news.summary: CapitalG led the Series C, which will fund LangSmith, LangChain's platform for running, evaluating and governing AI agents built with any framework. The company says over 7,000 organizations use LangSmith and plans a launch event on Nov. 20.

news.title: Mirendil raises a $1B Series A for agent-run AI research
news.summary: Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital led the round for the startup founded by former Anthropic researchers. Its products are Lor, an invite-only platform for delegating research tasks to agents, and an upcoming Fern 0.1 model.

news.title: SoftBank takes a $3.7B hit on data-center power gear it no longer needs
news.summary: The write-down on long-lead power equipment pushed SoftBank to a roughly $7B quarterly loss, its first in nearly two years. Its CFO warned that further procurement changes could bring more losses.

papers.title: ActWorld-JEPA: Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models Meet Latent Planning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: A driving planner imagines the future each candidate path would cause and uses that to re-rank its options, reaching 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
ActWorld-JEPA helps a self-driving planner choose between its candidate paths by imagining, for each one, how the scene would unfold, and then nudging that path's score up or down.

## Background you need
An end-to-end driving system takes in camera images and directly outputs a path for the car, instead of chaining many hand-built modules. Many such planners first propose a set of candidate paths and give each a score. A world model is a part of the system that predicts what the scene will look like next. A JEPA (joint-embedding predictive architecture) is a kind of world model that predicts compact internal summaries of the future, not full pictures, which is cheaper and focuses on meaning.

## The problem
Predicting the future well is not the same as choosing well. A model could forecast accurately under every option and still pick a poor one. Picture merging onto a highway: "keep speed" and "slow down" are both easy to predict, but they leave different gaps for the merging car. The planner has to weigh that outcome against the progress lost by braking. Earlier JEPA-style driving models mostly trained the forecast and hoped good decisions would follow.

## The idea
Think of a chess player who, before committing, plays each candidate move forward in their head and asks, "Does the position I end up in agree with what I was trying to do?" ActWorld-JEPA does this for every candidate path. It imagines the future that path would cause, compares the plan with that imagined future, and makes a small, capped correction to the original score.

## How it works
1. **Propose options.** A base planner suggests 32 possible paths, each with 8 waypoints covering the next 4 seconds, plus a starting score for each.
2. **Imagine each future (PC-JEPA).** A small network turns each path into a summary of its intent, both overall and step by step. A predictor then rolls the scene forward in time, one step at a time, guided by that intent. A gated attention step (a learned filter deciding how much to borrow) merges the imagined future with the current scene.
3. **Compare plan and outcome (R³).** The system checks where the plan's features and the imagined future agree and where they differ. A small network turns that comparison into a score correction and a confidence value.
4. **Adjust, don't replace.** The final score is the original score plus a bounded correction scaled by confidence. The car then picks the top-scoring path. The path's shape is never changed, only its ranking.
5. **Training.** The imagined future is pushed toward a summary of what actually happened next in the recorded data. A selection loss rewards picking the path closest to what a human driver did. None of this future information is used when driving.

## Results
On the NAVSIM v1 benchmark, which replays real scenes and scores paths on safety, comfort and progress (PDMS, higher is better), ActWorld-JEPA scored 94.1. That edges out PlanWAM (93.8) and Drive-JEPA (93.7), and clearly beats DiffusionDrive (88.1). On the harder NAVSIM v2 "navhard" split it scored 42.7 versus 37.7 for a reproduced Drive-JEPA. On nuScenes it cut average path error to 1.20 meters and predicted collisions to 0.76%, better than recent rivals around 1.37–1.48 m and 0.86–0.90%. It runs at 21 frames per second. In ablations, the imagination step alone lifted the base score from 87.1 to 90.5, and the comparison step took it to 94.1.

## Why it matters
Self-driving teams increasingly use world models, but turning forecasts into better choices is the hard part. This paper shows one concrete, fairly cheap way to do that: score each option by its imagined consequences. The same "imagine, compare, adjust" pattern could apply to robots or other agents that pick among candidate actions.

## Caveats
The headline 94.1 score was tuned using aggregate feedback from the same test set, so it is not a clean held-out number. Reranking cannot invent a good path if none of the 32 candidates is good. If the imagined futures are wrong, the corrections can be wrong too. All tests are open-loop or replayed simulations; nothing was tested on real roads or with traffic that reacts to the car.

## Key terms
- **End-to-end driving:** one neural network maps sensor input to a planned path.
- **Candidate trajectories:** the set of possible paths the planner chooses among.
- **World model:** a component that predicts how the scene will change.
- **JEPA:** a world model that predicts compact summaries of the future rather than images.
- **Reranking:** adjusting the order of options after an initial scoring.
- **PDMS:** NAVSIM's driving score combining safety checks, comfort and progress.

papers.title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
papers.tldr: Keeps a 2–3-bit model on the GPU and streams just the extra precision that matters from RAM or SSD, lifting a 2-bit Qwen3-8B from 11% to 47% on AIME with no extra GPU memory.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
StrataFlux makes heavily compressed language models almost as accurate as their uncompressed versions by keeping a tiny core on the graphics card and streaming in extra precision, only where it matters, from the computer's main memory or disk.

## Background you need
A large language model needs two big things in fast GPU memory (the graphics card's own memory): its weights (the learned numbers that define it) and its KV cache (the model's short-term memory of the text it has already read). Quantization shrinks both by storing each number with fewer bits, such as 2 or 3 bits instead of 16. That saves memory and speeds up text generation, which is mostly limited by how fast data can be read. Computers also have slower but much larger storage: main memory (RAM) and SSDs.

## The problem
Squeezing a model down to 2 bits costs accuracy, sometimes badly. For example, a 2-bit Qwen3-8B model solves only 11% of AIME math problems. The usual fix is to keep more precision somewhere slower and fetch it. But fetching from RAM or disk means the GPU sits idle waiting. So people choose between a small, fast, worse model and a bigger, slower, better one. This matters most on consumer GPUs and laptops, where memory is tight.

## The idea
Imagine a chef with a tiny counter and a big pantry. The basic ingredients sit on the counter. Instead of hauling the whole pantry over, an assistant brings only the few special items the next dish needs, timed to arrive just before the chef reaches for them. StrataFlux keeps the low-bit model on the GPU (the counter) and streams small "refinement bits" from RAM or SSD (the pantry) for the parts of the computation that matter most right now.

## How it works
1. **Store corrections separately.** For weights, it keeps extra correction values that undo rounding error. For the KV cache, it stores a few extra bits that pick a more exact value inside each coarse rounding range.
2. **Pick what matters.** Not every number is equally important. It ranks weight channels by how strongly they are activated, and past tokens by how much attention they get. Only the top slice gets refined. The corrections are also fitted to make up for the parts left out.
3. **Fetch early, apply late.** For some layers it predicts which channels will matter from the previous layer and starts the transfer early. For others it applies the correction a little later. Either way, the transfer has time to finish.
4. **Overlap and reuse.** Transfers run alongside the main computation. Because the same channels and tokens tend to be picked again on the next word, fetched bits are cached and reused.
5. **Auto-tune.** A tuner picks how much to refine for each model and machine, within a set speed budget (usually at most 5% slower).

## Results
With 2-bit weights, Llama-3.1-8B's perplexity (a measure of how surprised the model is by real text; lower is better) improved from 9.46 to 8.40. It kept 95.4% of the compressed model's speed on an RTX 5090. With both weights and KV cache at 2 bits, Qwen3-8B's AIME score rose from 11.0% to 47.1%, using no extra GPU memory. At a 128,000-token context, a 3-bit-weight, 2-bit-cache Llama matched the accuracy and speed of vLLM's standard 4-bit-weight, 8-bit-cache setup using about half the GPU memory. Comparisons included AWQ, KIVI, KVQuant, DecDEC, ShadowKV and others.

## Why it matters
It loosens the link between "how much fits on my GPU" and "how good the model is". People running models on gaming GPUs, small workstations, or laptops could get much better answers from the same hardware. It also offers a use for idle RAM and fast SSDs that most machines already have.

## Caveats
There is a speed cost that grows with batch size: about 19–25% lower throughput when serving 16 requests at once. Each model, quantizer and machine needs its own tuning run. The refinement bits take extra RAM or disk space. The system is a research prototype built in llama.cpp, tested on a limited set of models and platforms.

## Key terms
- **Quantization:** storing numbers with fewer bits to save memory, at some cost in accuracy.
- **KV cache:** stored information about earlier tokens so the model need not recompute it.
- **Refinement bits:** extra precision that sharpens a low-bit value when fetched.
- **Memory hierarchy:** the tiers of storage from fast and small (GPU) to slow and large (RAM, SSD).
- **Perplexity:** how well a model predicts real text; lower means better.
- **Throughput:** how many tokens the system produces per second.

papers.title: Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Grouping a prompt's keys into a few large meaning-based clusters makes long-context attention 2–3× faster with no retraining.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper speeds up language models on very long inputs, without any retraining, by sorting the model's stored memory into a few big topic groups and letting each new word read only the groups it needs.

## Background you need
In a transformer, attention is the step where each word (a "query") looks back at every earlier word (stored as "keys" and "values") to decide what matters. For a million-token input, that is a huge amount of reading. Sparse attention means reading only a selected subset of earlier words. Work splits into prefill (reading the whole prompt once) and decoding (writing the answer one token at a time). Hybrid models mix normal attention layers with cheaper layer types.

## The problem
Long documents, codebases and chat histories now reach hundreds of thousands of tokens. Full attention makes prefill slow and every generated token expensive. Many training-free sparse methods group keys into small blocks of neighboring positions and pick the best blocks. Small blocks are precise, but scoring many of them costs time, so each query ends up reading fewer tokens. Nearby tokens are also not always related in meaning.

## The idea
Think of a library. Instead of shelving books strictly by arrival date, you sort them into a handful of large subject sections. A reader first glances at each section's sign, then walks only to the relevant sections and reads the actual books there. Because there are few signs, glancing is cheap. That saved time lets the reader look at more books overall.

## How it works
1. **Build an index per prompt.** When a prompt arrives, its keys are grouped into large semantic clusters. A cluster can mix tokens from far-apart positions if they are similar.
2. **Score the signs.** Each query compares itself with each cluster's centroid (the cluster's average key) and picks the clusters it needs.
3. **Read the real content.** Inside the chosen clusters, the query attends to the original, uncompressed keys and values, so no information is approximated away.
4. **Batch similar queries.** Queries that pick the same cluster are processed together, which keeps prefill efficient on the GPU.
5. **Spend savings on coverage.** Because scoring few large clusters is cheap, each query can afford a bigger token budget in the same time.

## Results
The authors tested two hybrid models, Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Counting the cost of building and using the index, the whole model ran 2.3–2.4× faster than dense attention for prefill and 1.7–2.0× faster for decoding at 512,000 tokens. At one million tokens, prefill was 2.9–3.0× faster. A prompt that took 30 seconds to read would take roughly 10. The 35B model stayed close to dense-attention accuracy on five RULER long-context tasks up to one million tokens, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR up to 256,000 tokens. The key finding is that large clusters with a bigger budget beat small clusters with a smaller budget on both speed and accuracy.

## Why it matters
Long-context features are expensive to serve, and this method needs no retraining, so it can be added to existing models. Faster prefill means shorter waits before an answer starts on long documents. The result also challenges the habit of using small, position-based blocks for sparse attention.

## Caveats
The smaller 4B model lost accuracy, mainly on tasks that require retrieving several separate facts at once. The authors note it still beat a dense 2B model running at similar speed, but the loss is real. Tests cover two models from one family on one GPU type. The index must be rebuilt for each new prompt. Results on other architectures or shorter contexts are not reported.

## Key terms
- **Attention:** how each token weighs earlier tokens when computing its output.
- **Sparse attention:** reading only a chosen subset of earlier tokens.
- **Prefill / decoding:** reading the prompt versus generating the answer token by token.
- **Cluster centroid:** the average of a group's keys, used as its summary.
- **Training-free:** works on an existing model without changing its weights.
- **Hybrid model:** a model mixing full attention layers with cheaper layer types.

papers.title: KernelMutate: Mutation-Guided Validation of Generated GPU Kernels
papers.tldr: Stronger testing shows that many AI-generated CUDA kernels accepted by a few random checks still fail, including 136 of 548 with real FP32 errors.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
KernelMutate checks how trustworthy the usual tests for AI-written GPU code really are, and finds that many kernels that "pass" are actually wrong in ways those tests never look for.

## Background you need
A GPU kernel is a small, highly tuned program that runs one operation, such as a matrix multiply, on a graphics card. Language models are now used to write such kernels automatically, and a generated kernel is accepted if it gives the same answers as a trusted reference. That comparison is called differential testing: run both versions on some random inputs and check that the outputs match. FP32 means ordinary 32-bit floating-point numbers; lower-precision types such as 16-bit numbers are faster but round more.

## The problem
In practice, a generated kernel is often accepted after only a handful of random tests. Passing five random checks does not prove the kernel is safe to drop into real software. It may break on unusual shapes, on edge values, or when run with a different number type. Teams that report "X% of generated kernels are correct" may be counting kernels that would fail in use. That inflates progress claims and risks shipping silent errors.

## The idea
The paper treats the tests themselves as the thing under examination. It is like checking a smoke detector by deliberately lighting small, known fires. If the detector misses some, you learn exactly where it is blind. KernelMutate plants known bugs (mutations) and runs much stronger checks, then counts how many problems the cheap tests let through.

## How it works
1. **Collect candidates.** The authors gather 838 CUDA kernels produced by code generators, together with released implementations and their replacement tests.
2. **Run the cheap baseline.** They apply the common practice of five random test draws and record which kernels it accepts.
3. **Run a full suite.** They then test accepted kernels much more thoroughly. Each failure comes with a "witness": a concrete input that exposes it. Witnesses are sorted by domain, such as a true failure at native FP32 precision versus one that only appears with lower-precision number types.
4. **Try a cheaper, guided suite.** A source-guided approach reads the kernel's code to choose which probes to run, aiming for the same coverage at lower cost.
5. **Rank probes.** On tasks held out from tuning, they test which short list of probes catches the most problems.

## Results
The five-draw baseline accepted 548 of the 838 candidates. The full suite found real FP32 failures in 136 of those accepted kernels. It found a further 362 with problems that show up only under particular number types, mostly tied to low-precision behavior that GPU vendors do not formally guarantee. The source-guided method covered the same 692 candidates at 26.1% lower cost. But for 16 kernels it found only number-type evidence where the full suite had caught a native FP32 failure, so cheaper is not free. For probe lists, a single global top-eight list matched 51 of 75 held-out probes, versus 48 for lists tailored to each kernel class.

## Why it matters
Automatic kernel writing is a fast-growing area, and leaderboards depend on what "correct" means. This work suggests reported success rates can be much too high when testing is light. The authors argue that papers and tools should report what kind of evidence each check produced and how much of the behavior was covered, not just yield and cost. That would make results comparable and safer to deploy.

## Caveats
These are offline measurements on one collection of CUDA candidates, not improvements to a deployed test system. Many findings concern low-precision behavior where there is no agreed vendor standard for what counts as a bug. The cheaper guided suite misses some serious failures. Whether the same patterns hold for other GPU languages or newer hardware is not shown.

## Key terms
- **GPU kernel:** a small program that runs one operation in parallel on a graphics card.
- **Differential testing:** checking a new program against a trusted one on the same inputs.
- **Mutation testing:** planting known bugs to measure how well a test suite catches them.
- **Witness:** a specific input that demonstrates a failure.
- **FP32:** standard 32-bit floating-point numbers.
- **Low precision:** smaller number formats that are faster but round more.

papers.title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
papers.tldr: Splitting a robot policy into a slow vision-language 'thinker' and a fast action controller trained on stale memory keeps robots reactive as models grow.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper lets a robot keep moving quickly by splitting its "brain" into a slow thinker that updates a short memory now and then and a fast controller that acts many times per second using that memory.

## Background you need
Many new robot arms are driven by vision-language-action models: one network that looks at camera images, reads an instruction like "put the bowl in the drawer", and outputs motor commands. These models are built on top of a large vision-language model (a network trained to understand pictures and text together). Bigger vision-language models understand scenes better, but each answer takes longer to compute.

## The problem
In today's designs the big model and the action generator run one after the other, in the same loop. The robot can only react as fast as both steps together. So every time the model gets bigger, the robot gets slower to respond. That is fine for a still tabletop. It fails when an object rolls, gets bumped, or is moved mid-task. Simply running the two parts at different speeds creates a new problem: the fast part is now acting on information that may be a second or two old.

## The idea
Think of a rally driver and a co-driver. The co-driver reads the route notes and calls out what is ahead every few seconds. The driver steers continuously using their own eyes, guided by the latest call. The driver never waits for the co-driver to finish talking. Asynchronous Robot Policies (ARP) works the same way: a slow "semantic loop" gives guidance, and a fast "action loop" does the steering. The trick is training the driver to cope with calls that are slightly out of date.

## How it works
1. **Slow loop builds a memory.** The large vision-language model looks at the scene and instruction. The authors take its internal working state from several layers and squeeze it into a small, fixed-size memory. The memory is tagged with how old it is.
2. **Fast loop acts.** A small transformer called the Vision-Action Expert sees fresh camera images (including a wrist camera) and the robot's joint positions. At every layer it looks up the latest memory. It generates a short chunk of actions with flow matching (a method that gradually turns random noise into a smooth motion).
3. **Training on stale memory.** During training, the current camera frame is paired on purpose with memory computed from an earlier frame. The delay is sometimes zero and sometimes random up to a set maximum. The model is also told how stale the memory is and how much compute delay to expect.
4. **Smooth hand-offs.** When a new action chunk is planned, the first few steps are copied from the chunk already being executed. This avoids jerky jumps between plans.

## Results
On the LIBERO simulated benchmark, ARP reached 84.8% average success with a 1-billion-parameter backbone and 89.3% with 8 billion, versus 80.2% and 82.7% for comparable π0-style baselines. The gap widens when things move. When the target object is shifted 5 cm mid-episode, ARP succeeds 51.5% of the time versus 9.5% for the baseline. In a "dynamic bump" test, where a moving target is suddenly knocked, ARP scores about 45% versus 13–20%. When the big model was slowed to update only twice per second, ARP kept 81.8% success. Without the stale-memory training, success fell to 2%. On real Franka arm tasks, the authors report 18% higher success and 20% shorter execution than the baseline. Smooth hand-offs cut jerky motion by 39.4%.

## Why it matters
Robot makers want both smarter models and faster reflexes. This design means a bigger "thinking" model does not automatically make the robot sluggish. It could let home or factory robots catch, dodge, or recover from bumps while still following complex instructions. It also lets the heavy model run on slower or shared hardware.

## Caveats
Several key tests (the object shift and the bump) are benchmarks the authors built themselves. The real-robot study is small: three tasks with 10 trials each. On the larger RoboLab simulation, ARP (20.0%) beats a similar-size rival but trails π0.5 (37.9%), which was trained on much more private data. How rarely the slow loop can update before things break is not yet known.

## Key terms
- **Vision-language-action model:** a network that turns images and an instruction into robot motor commands.
- **Latency:** the delay between seeing something and acting on it.
- **Semantic memory:** a compact summary of the scene and goal produced by the big model.
- **Staleness:** how old that summary is when the fast controller uses it.
- **Flow matching:** a training method that learns to turn random noise into a realistic action sequence step by step.
- **Action chunk:** a short planned sequence of motor commands executed in a row.

papers.title: VIGOR: Benchmarking Visual Rationale Correctness in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A benchmark that checks whether image-reading AI models actually look at the right pixels when explaining their answers, and finds they often do not.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
VIGOR is a test that checks whether AI models that read images actually look at the right part of the picture when they explain an answer, not just whether the answer is right.

## Background you need
A multimodal large language model is a chatbot-style AI that can take both images and text as input, then answer questions about them. Such models often give a rationale: a short explanation like "the cup is about to fall because it sits on the table's edge". Grounding means linking each idea in that explanation to the exact pixels in the image it refers to. A benchmark is a shared test set researchers use to compare models.

## The problem
Today these models are mostly scored on whether the final answer is correct. A correct answer can still rest on the wrong evidence. A model might say "the dog is running" because dogs in photos often run, not because it saw motion in this image. That matters for trust. A medical or safety tool that is right for the wrong reasons may fail without warning on the next case. Checking evidence by hand is slow, so few large tests measure it.

## The idea
Think of a math teacher who marks not just the final number but also the working. VIGOR gives credit only when the model's stated reasons point to the right visual evidence. It asks, in the authors' framing, whether models "look at what they say".

## How it works
1. **Break explanations into concepts.** Each rationale is written as a set of explicit visual concepts. The concepts span several levels: basic properties such as color or texture, middle-level structures, whole objects and their parts, and high-level motion and relations between things.
2. **Attach pixels to each concept.** Every concept is paired with a pixel-level mask showing where in the image it appears.
3. **Build the data automatically.** Where existing datasets already have detailed labels, the pipeline reuses them. Where labels are missing, it generates candidate regions and then keeps only those that pass a cautious check by another multimodal model.
4. **Compare evidence.** For each concept a model mentions, the authors extract which part of the image the model relied on and compare it with the annotated ground truth.

## Results
The authors report that current multimodal models show limited visual rationale correctness. In other words, their explanations often do not line up with the right regions of the image. The failures also differ by level: the ways models go wrong on basic properties are not the same as on objects or on motion and relations. The public abstract and conference listing give these as qualitative findings and do not state headline scores, model names or dataset size, so we do not quote numbers here.

## Why it matters
As image-reading AI moves into areas like medical imaging, inspection and driving assistance, being right for the right reason becomes important. VIGOR gives researchers a scalable way to measure that, and a pipeline to build more such data. Splitting results by concept level can show developers exactly which kind of visual reasoning to fix. It could also be used to train models to ground their explanations better.

## Caveats
Our summary is based on the paper's abstract and conference listing; the detailed numbers are in the full paper. Much of the labeling is automatic, and the check that filters labels is itself an AI model, so some ground truth may be imperfect. Measuring "where a model looked" depends on the extraction method chosen, which may not perfectly reflect how the model reasons internally. The benchmark tests explanations, not whether better grounding improves real-world outcomes.

## Key terms
- **Multimodal large language model:** an AI that handles both images and text.
- **Rationale:** the model's explanation for its answer.
- **Grounding:** linking a word or idea to the exact image region it describes.
- **Pixel-level mask:** an outline marking which pixels belong to something.
- **Benchmark:** a shared test used to compare models fairly.
